title: Proper Learning of Shallow All-to-All Quantum Circuits
abstract: This work considers a variation on the problem of learning shallow quantum circuits. Given query access to the circuit, as well as knowledge of its gate layout, we consider the task of learning the specific gates used in the circuit, producing an operationally-equivalent circuit matching this structure. Building on recent work for learning Haar random brickwork circuits, we identify a meta-algorithmic framework for learning broad classes of circuits based on iterative local gate inversions at the front and back of the circuit. We apply these techniques to study random, all-to-all, two-local circuits, and provide analytical and numerical evidence that this ensemble undergoes a sharp learnability transition at depth $d^* \sim \log_2 n + \log_2\log_2 n$ in the large size limit, based on an analysis of lightcone growth. These results have implications for recently proposed quantum cryptographic schemes based on the difficulty of circuit learning, though there are important distinctions with respect to our setting that suggest avenues for future study.
summary: This paper develops a framework to determine the specific gates within a shallow quantum circuit by probing its causal structure using lightcones. It finds that random, all-to-all circuits undergo a sharp transition in learnability at a depth scaling as $\log_2 n + \log_2 \log_2 n$. This result has implications for understanding the inherent complexity of quantum circuits.
main_problem: The work addresses the problem of 'proper learning' of shallow quantum circuits, meaning determining the specific gates used given query access and knowledge of the circuit's structure.
main_result: For random, all-to-all, two-local circuits, the ensemble exhibits a sharp learnability transition at a depth $d^* \sim \log_2 n + \log_2 \log_2 n$ in the large size limit.
method: The authors develop a meta-algorithmic framework based on iterative local gate inversions at the front and back of the circuit, utilizing lightcone analysis to probe causal structure.
model_or_system: The model involves unitary quantum circuits acting on $n$ qubits, specifically analyzing random, all-to-all, two-local circuits. The analysis uses concepts like lightcones and causal boundaries derived from the circuit graph structure.
key_observables: Lightcone growth, the learnability threshold $d^*$, and the causal boundaries defined by lightcone differences.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($d$), number of qubits ($n$), and the specific structure (all-to-all, two-local) of the random circuit ensemble.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the circuit is 'shallow' (low depth) and builds upon prior work for brickwork circuits, while also distinguishing its setting from quantum cryptography.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the correspondence between standard quantum circuit notation and a directed graph representation; Figure 2 schematically shows the learning algorithm using forward and backward lightcones.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of circuit learning, develops the lightcone diagnostic tool, and applies this framework to analyze the learnability transition for specific random circuit ensembles, culminating in the determination of the threshold depth $d^*$.
why_interesting: The analysis of circuit learnability thresholds provides fundamental insights into the complexity and structure of quantum computations, which is relevant for understanding the limits of quantum information processing and potential cryptographic security.

Colored lines indicate lightcones originating from ρ (forward) or σ (backward) in the presence of G (orange) or with G removed (purple). Figure 5: Example of a 6 qubit, 4 layer circuit with 2-local gates that cannot be learned by forward- only or backward-only pass using single-gate local inversions. Here, “learning” means there is always an available pivot gate (outer gate with good lightcones), and we tacitly assume this allows for some removal procedure. Learning proceeds in one direction until no more pivots are present on that side (front or back), and at that point one switches to learning the other direction. Although a single forward or backward pass cannot clear the circuit, it can be learned using alternations of forward and backward lightcone protocols. See subcaptions for additional details.
